label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
in_my_words: The agents each had a job and a page of rules, woke up on a timer, and had a second agent check their plan and their work, so the person could walk away and still trust what came back.
why: I like the little personalities and the idea of a brake, and the 'Do this now' boxes are things I could actually try. But words like repository, commit, debrief and gate keep appearing without help, and I keep wondering whether this is for people who write code. I would read one more chapter if it stays about people-like characters and gives me a step.

by_section.why: Short, concrete and easy to picture. A blank start feels like my own first build. 'Repository' is not explained, but I can guess.
by_section.quote: A new repository with a licence, a short read-me and nothing else.

by_section.why: Four characters with a one-word mood each (happy, fussy, night owl) made them easy to tell apart. The 'Words for this page' box helped with conductor, hold and check. The empty chair is a nice hook.
by_section.quote: Remember the empty chair: it comes back at the end.

by_section.why: The picture is described in words only, and 'the agent tool', 'the build', 'the ordinary end' and 'Wardley map' pile up. This is where I feel it might be for programmers. I only half get why it matters.
by_section.quote: the bottom of the chain was already ordinary, so the top could be built in a day.

by_section.section: The clock and the five steps
by_section.why: The five steps in plain words are the clearest explanation of the factory. 'Wake', 'reviewer' and 'debrief' are defined. I wanted to know what the brake physically is.
by_section.quote: It looks slow written down. The checking is what let nobody watch.

by_section.why: I follow that a checker caught a slip, but 'changed a file outside its own page of rules' and 'debrief or record' are vague to me. The line about a second reading is the part that stuck.
by_section.quote: a second reading, not a second identity.

by_section.why: Quick, gives me the count (six agents, a clock, a brake) and a feeling of momentum. The researcher is introduced as the one who says no, which is a good promise.
by_section.quote: A factory that could run without me. From just after four, it did.

by_section.why: This is the step I can take tomorrow. It tells me I do not need six agents. I would like an example of a rules page.
by_section.quote: You do not need six agents. You need the page the first one read.

by_section.why: The claim is exciting but the section is mostly a picture description and a list of how it was held together. 'Trigger' and 'wakes' are used without help here. I wanted the payoff sooner.
by_section.quote: For nine hours I started nothing.

by_section.why: My favourite. An agent argues with its checker and wins, and the checker admits it. I understood every beat. The researcher feels like a person.
by_section.quote: I am not asking for an exception; I am asking you to read the line again.

by_section.why: Four small mistakes, each owned. The designer's 'I specified it wrong' is human. The '@' on the name is a bit insider-ish, but it is funny. It starts to feel like a list, though.
by_section.quote: Nobody was watching, and they argued, sent work back, owned their mistakes and kept the books.

by_section.why: Lots of times and commit-style detail (15:07, 18:37), and 'ported' and 'priority' are jargon. The idea of looking, asking, getting a change and looking again is the same as what I did in my own build, which I liked. The cast filling up is hard to follow without the picture.
by_section.quote: I looked, I asked, they changed it, I looked again.

by_section.why: Clear stakes: the helper told the boss his claim was wrong, and he kept his line but kept the objection on the record too. That makes me trust the team. The storyteller's voice is not very different from the others, though.
by_section.quote: a story that hides the strongest argument against it is not one I want to tell.

by_section.why: I can get the gist (it would not accept a second-hand yes) but the setup is thin: what is a page of rules being marked agreed? Studio has had almost no introduction, so I do not know who this is.
by_section.quote: My session would not take a relayed word for his, so I asked him myself.

by_section.why: A small step I could do today with a friend. The advice to change it and hand it over again fits the loop.
by_section.quote: Give one small thing to somebody else today, and write down what they asked for differently.

best_line: I am not asking for an exception; I am asking you to read the line again.
worst_moment: 'The map, before its name' in chapter 2: Wardley map, ordinary end, the agent tool, the build and the check all land at once with only a description of a picture, and it is where I felt the book might be for programmers.
cut: Shorten 'The map, before its name' to two or three sentences, drop one of the four 'sent back' stories (the '@' one or the second request), and trim the time stamps in 'The creator comes back'.
notes: The italic stage directions and the 'Words for this page' boxes are what keep me in. More of those for repository, commit, trigger and brake would help. The storyteller, motion and studio arrive as names only, so I cannot tell them apart yet. Some Figure descriptions read like notes to the designer, and I cannot see the pictures, so I lose what they were meant to carry.
